how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.title: How to Choose a Forex Broker in 2026: The Complete Guide
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s0.p0: Every forex broker's homepage says roughly the same thing: tight spreads, fast execution, award-winning platforms. This makes it difficult to compare brokers based on marketing copy alone. The good news is that the things that truly determine whether a broker can be trusted with your money are verifiable — regulation, cost structure, platform quality, and how the broker handles withdrawal requests. This guide covers each of these in the order we actually check them.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s0.p1: This is not investment advice, and nothing here tells you which specific broker you should choose. It is a framework you can apply to any broker — the four criteria directly align with how we score each broker in our own rankings, meaning you can use this guide not just to trust us, but to check our numbers yourself.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.heading: 1. Start with regulation, not spreads
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.p0: Regulation is the most critical filter because it determines what happens when something goes wrong — a platform outage during a volatile move, a dispute over an executed price, or in the worst-case scenario, the broker itself facing financial distress.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.p1: Not all regulators offer the same protection. Tier-1 regulators — the UK's FCA, Australia's ASIC, Cyprus's CySEC (an EU regulator), and a few others — require brokers to segregate client funds from company funds, maintain minimum capital reserves, and in some jurisdictions, participate in a compensation scheme that pays back clients if the broker goes bankrupt. Offshore regulators (common jurisdictions include Mauritius, Seychelles, Belize, and BVI) also have real licensing processes, but capital requirements and supervision are generally lighter, and they usually lack an investor compensation scheme behind them.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.p2: This does not mean an offshore-regulated broker is automatically a scam — many operate honestly for years. It means the regulatory safety net beneath you is thinner, making issues (a slow withdrawal, a disputed trade) more likely to become a problem you have to solve on your own rather than something a regulator steps in to address.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.l0: Check how many regulators a broker holds licenses under and in which jurisdictions — a single Tier-1 license is meaningfully different from zero licenses.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.l1: A broker regulated in your home jurisdiction (or a Tier-1 country) provides you with a realistic avenue for complaints if something goes wrong.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s1.l2: Multiple offshore licenses and zero Tier-1 coverage is not an automatic disqualification on its own, but it is a pattern to weigh carefully — evaluate it alongside the other three checks below.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s2.heading: 2. Calculate the true cost of a trade, not just the advertised spread
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s2.p0: "Low spread" is the most common marketing claim in this industry, and also the easiest to present deceptively. A broker advertising a 0.0 pip EUR/USD spread on a Raw/ECN account almost always charges a separate commission per lot — the total cost can be higher than a "standard" account with a wider spread and no commission. To compare accounts honestly, you need to add spread and commission together.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s2.p1: Beyond spread and commission, check: overnight swap/rollover rates if you hold positions past the daily cutoff, inactivity fees if you do not trade for a while, and deposit or withdrawal fees if any (most reputable brokers do not charge these, which is a useful signal in itself).
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s2.p2: The minimum deposit amount matters not in terms of cost, but in terms of how much room you have to manage risk properly. A $5 minimum deposit looks attractive, but trading with too little capital relative to position size is one of the most common ways new traders blow up their accounts — this is usually not the broker's fault, but a broker offering products suited only for over-leveraged micro accounts is not doing you any favors either.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s3.heading: 3. Test the platform before depositing into a live account
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s3.p0: MetaTrader 4 and MetaTrader 5 remain the most widely used retail platforms because they are broker-agnostic — even if you switch brokers, your chart settings, indicators, and expert advisors (EAs) move with you. cTrader is a common second option preferred by some ECN-focused brokers. Many brokers also build their own web or mobile platforms on top of these; this can be more polished, but it ties your workflow to that single broker.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s3.p1: The only way to truly evaluate a platform is to open a demo account and use it: check execution speed under normal and volatile conditions, whether one-click trading and stop-loss placement feel reliable, and if the charting and indicator suite meets your strategy's needs. A broker's platform is something you will interact with every trading day — spending twenty minutes to test it before depositing real money is worth it.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s4.heading: 4. Withdrawal speed is the most honest signal a broker gives you
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s4.p0: Deposits are always fast — every broker wants your money to arrive quickly. The true test happens with withdrawals, because a broker experiencing cash flow issues or aiming to discourage withdrawals will slow the process down, add unexpected verification hurdles, or hide the procedure in fine print.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s4.p1: You don't need to guess. Independent review sites collect real user reports, and recurring withdrawal complaints are one of the clearest red flags a broker can have — far clearer than anything a marketing page will tell you. If you are evaluating a broker we haven't reviewed, search for it first in our own Broker Search tool, then check its name alongside "withdrawal" on an independent review site before depositing into a live account.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s4.p2: This is precisely why we maintain a dedicated risk warnings page for brokers with prominent independent trust scores or complaint patterns — this page is generated from the exact same review data, not from a separate opinion.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s5.heading: How this aligns with the FXPARTNER Index
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s5.p0: Every broker we review receives a score from 0-10 across these exact four axes — Regulation, Cost, Platform, and Withdrawal — which are averaged into a single FXPARTNER Index. The Regulation axis is calculated directly from the number and tier of licenses held by the broker; Cost and Platform are editorial assessments based on the criteria above; Withdrawal is scored based on verifiable signals from independent reviews, drawing from the same sources mentioned above. A broker with no negative withdrawal signals receives a neutral score on that axis, not a default positive score — we do not assume in favor of a broker.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s5.p1: You can see the full breakdown, including the rationale behind each score, on any broker's review page — we explicitly display the axis scores alongside the final number so you can check our work.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s6.heading: A practical checklist before opening an account
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s6.l0: Verify at least one regulator relevant to your own country, preferably one at Tier-1 level.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s6.l1: Add up the spread + commission for the account type you will actually use, not the cheapest account type advertised.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s6.l2: Open a demo account and make a few trades to test order execution and platform compatibility.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s6.l3: Before depositing money into a live account, search the broker's name alongside "withdrawal" on an independent review site.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s6.l4: When verifying a broker's real-world behavior, start with an amount you are fully prepared to lose — this applies even to well-regulated brokers.
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s7.heading: Where to look from here
how-to-choose-a-forex-broker.s7.p0: If you want a shortcut where all of this is pre-applied to real brokers, our broker rankings page puts every listed broker through exactly this framework, and our category pages group brokers according to what matters most to you — brokers with low spreads, high leverage, or the strongest regulatory coverage. If you are evaluating a broker not listed here, the checklist above works just as well on its own.

fomc-faiz-karari-fed-baskani-konusmasi.t: FOMC Interest Rate Decision and FED Chair's Speech: What Awaits the Markets Today?
fomc-faiz-karari-fed-baskani-konusmasi.s: Global Markets' Eyes on the FED
Today, the focus of financial markets is on the interest rate decision to be announced by the US Federal Reserve (FOMC), followed by the press conference of the FED Chair.

These two developments are of great importance not only for the US economy, but also for gold, foreign exchange, equities, and cryptocurrency markets. As sharp price movements may occur in the markets following the decision, investors need to pay extra attention to risk management.
What Time Will the FOMC Rate Decision Be Announced?
In addition to the interest rate, the wording used in the statement and the messages given by the FED Chair will be decisive for market direction.
What Are Market Expectations?
The vast majority of economists expect the FED to keep its policy rate unchanged at its current level.

However, for investors, the main issue will be the signals the FED gives for upcoming meetings rather than the rate decision itself. Answers to the following questions in particular will be closely followed:
Is there a possibility of an interest rate cut during the remainder of the year?
How will the FED assess inflation?
Will new messages be delivered regarding the labor market?
Have economic growth expectations changed?
How Could Gold (XAU/USD) Be Affected?
If Hawkish Messages Emerge — If the FED emphasizes its determination in fighting inflation and states that interest rates could remain high for a long time:
If Dovish Messages Emerge — If the FED leaves the door open to future interest rate cuts:
Gold may experience selling pressure.
The US Dollar may gain strength.
Bond yields may rise.
Pressure may be seen in equity markets.
Which Pairs May Move in the Forex Market?
Since wide spreads and sudden price movements can occur in a short time, it is important for investors using high leverage to be cautious.
Will the Cryptocurrency Market Be Affected?
Yes. Bitcoin and other major crypto assets have become highly sensitive to FED decisions in recent years.
Messages indicating that interest rates will remain high for a long time may put pressure on risky assets. Conversely, softer (dovish) statements may lead to positive pricing in the crypto market.
What Should Investors Pay Attention To?
Keep trading volume lower than normal.
Do not neglect using stop-loss.
Be cautious against sharp movements in the first few minutes.
Be sure to follow the press conference as well; the main direction often forms here.
Instead of trading based on a single statement, waiting for the market's initial reaction to settle may be healthier.
Conclusion
Today's FOMC interest rate decision and the FED Chair's statements are among the most important economic developments of the week, and even the month.

Rather than whether the interest rate changes or not, the FED's forward-looking messages will determine the direction of pricing in global markets. In particular, investors trading in gold, dollar, forex pairs, equities, and cryptocurrency markets need to be prepared for high volatility during the announcement hours.
As FXPARTNER, we follow developments closely and will continue to regularly share with you the impacts of important economic events on the markets.
forex-risk-yonetimi-pozisyon-buyuklugu-s: Risk Management in Forex: Position Sizing and Stop-Loss Strategies

In Forex, beginners are often defeated not by their analysis, but by risk management. Even if you predicted the correct direction, if your position is too large relative to your account, a single adverse move can knock you out of the market entirely. This article addresses fundamental risk management rules that experienced investors apply almost automatically, but beginners mostly skip.
This is not a guarantee of winning — no risk management technique eliminates losses. The goal is to ensure that a single bad trade or a few consecutive losses do not permanently damage your account.
1. Think of risk per trade as a percentage of account size

Most experienced investors do not risk more than %1-2 of their account balance on a single trade. This is not the lot size, but the dollar/TL equivalent of the distance to the stop-loss. The %1 risk rule in a 10.000$ account means accepting a maximum loss of 100$ on any trade — whether the stop-loss is 20 pip or 80 pip away, position size is adjusted accordingly.

The power of this approach lies in the math: even if you suffer 10 consecutive losses with the %1 rule, you lose approximately %10 of your account — a recoverable level. If you keep position size fixed and do not adjust it according to the stop-loss, a few wide-stop trades can drain the account much faster.
2. Place the stop-loss according to the market, not an arbitrary number

A common mistake is placing the stop-loss according to a fixed number like "50 pip" — whereas the correct distance varies depending on the volatility of the traded instrument and recent support/resistance levels. While a 15 pip stop makes sense on a calm major pair, the same distance could be triggered instantly within the normal noise of the market on gold or a highly volatile crypto pair.

A practical method: placing the stop slightly beyond the recent swing high/low or a distinct support/resistance area — that is, allowing the price to "breathe" during its normal course and exiting only at the point where the scenario actually becomes invalid. Once the stop distance is determined, the position size is calculated to match the risk percentage in step 1 — the sequence works in this order, not the reverse.
3. Leverage is not risk — it is merely a multiplier

High leverage is not dangerous in itself; what is dangerous is using the maximum position size that leverage allows. A 1:500 leveraged account does not force you to open a large position — it simply allows you to open a large position with a small margin. Without risk management discipline, this is a way to accelerate losses.
In our article where we cover leverage in more detail, we discuss this difference and the leverage limits that vary by broker/country in greater depth.
4. Pay attention to correlation

Opening long positions simultaneously in EUR/USD, GBP/USD, and EUR/GBP might feel like three separate independent trades — but these pairs move with a high degree of correlation. When the market turns against you, all three start losing money at the same time; your actual risk is much higher than what you calculated per single trade. Evaluating the total directional exposure (net exposure) of your open positions is as important as evaluating individual trades.
A practical checklist
Before opening a trade, determine the dollar/TL amount you are willing to risk (1-2% of the account).
Place the stop-loss according to market structure, then calculate the position size accordingly.
Consider total exposure before opening multiple positions simultaneously in highly correlated pairs.
Set a maximum loss level upon reaching which in a day or week you will stop trading.
No rule guarantees against losses — this is a capital preservation framework, not a guarantee of profit.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.title: Technical Analysis or Fundamental Analysis? Using Both Together
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s0.p0: A common debate encountered in forex forums: "Does technical analysis work, or fundamental analysis?" In fact, this is a wrongly framed question. The two methods answer different questions, and many experienced investors use them together — one attempts to explain where the price might go, and the other why it might go there.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s1.heading: Technical analysis: what is the price itself telling us?
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s1.p0: Technical analysis is based on the assumption that past price movements and trading volume provide clues about future price behavior. Support/resistance levels, trendlines, moving averages (SMA/EMA), and indicators like RSI are the primary tools of this approach.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s1.p1: The strong side of technical analysis is that it provides concrete, measurable levels for entry/exit timing and risk management (determining where to place your stop-loss). Its weak side is that an unexpected news flow (for instance, a central bank decision) can invalidate technical levels instantly.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s2.heading: Fundamental analysis: what drives the price?
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s2.p0: Fundamental analysis evaluates the value of a currency through interest rates, inflation, employment data, growth figures, and central bank policies. For example, a central bank raising interest rates generally increases demand for that currency — because assets held in that currency offer higher returns.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s2.p1: The strength of fundamental analysis is that it allows you to understand the logic behind large and sustainable trends. Its weakness is that, while it answers the question "how will an interest rate decision affect the market," it does not answer the question "today, at what time, from which level" with the same clarity.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s3.heading: A practical way to use both together
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s3.p0: A common approach is this: determining the general direction (bias) with fundamental analysis, and timing entry/exit in that direction with technical analysis. For example, if central bank policies generally signal strengthening for a currency, evaluating technical pullback points as entry opportunities offers a more consistent framework than predicting direction by looking at indicators alone.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s3.p1: Following the economic calendar (such as interest rate decisions, inflation data, employment reports) is an integral part of this process — we discuss this topic in more detail in a separate article.
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s4.heading: Which method suits whom?
teknik-analiz-vs-temel-analiz.s4.p0: Short-term traders (intraday or scalping) usually focus on technical analysis, as decision times occur within hours or even minutes. For investors who hold position sizes for weeks/months, fundamental analysis is generally more decisive. For most investors, the ideal approach is not to choose one completely, but to assign a certain weight to both according to their own time horizon.
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.title: What is Leverage? Opportunities and Risks
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s0.p0: Leverage is one of the most highlighted features in forex brokers' marketing materials — expressions like "1:500 leverage" look attractive. But opening an account without understanding what leverage actually means and why it should be used cautiously is one of the most common ways to lose your capital much faster than necessary.
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s1.head: How does leverage work?
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s1.p1: This point is critical: leverage does not change the size of your profit/loss, it only reduces the margin required to open a position of the same size. So the real determining factor is the position size, not the leverage ratio itself.
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s2.head: Why is high leverage risky?
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s2.p0: Because high leverage makes it possible to open large positions with low margin, it can wipe out an account very quickly if used undisciplined. For example, if you put almost your entire account as margin into a single position with 1:500 leverage, even a small percentage price movement can consume your margin and lead to the automatic closure of your position (margin call/stop-out).
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s2.p1: This does not mean leverage is "bad" — professional investors also use high-leverage accounts. The difference is that they open the position determined according to the risk management rules discussed in our previous article (such as %1-2 risk per trade), not the maximum position allowed by leverage.
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s3.head: Leverage limits by country and broker
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s3.p0: Tier-1 regulators (such as UK FCA, Europe ESMA/CySEC) legally limit leverage caps for retail investors — usually around 1:30 on major pairs. Offshore licensed brokers can offer much higher leverage (1:500, or even 1:1000). The availability of high leverage is not a red flag in itself, but it is usually a sign of a lighter-regulated structure — we cover this balance in more detail in our broker selection guide.
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s4.head: Practical approach
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s4.l0: Think of leverage not as "how large a position can I open", but as "how little margin can I trade with".
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s4.l1: Set your position size according to your risk management rules, not according to the maximum allowed by leverage.
kaldirac-leverage-nedir-riskleri.s4.l2: If you are starting out, beginning with a low-to-medium leverage account reduces the risk of a margin call and makes the learning process less stressful.
trading-psikolojisi-duygusal-kararlar.ti: Trading Psychology: How to Avoid Emotional Decisions?
trading-psikolojisi-duygusal-kararlar.s0: There is a frequently repeated saying among experienced investors: "Trading is 80 percent psychology, 20 percent strategy." While the exact numbers are open to debate, the idea is correct — even a good strategy becomes useless when the person executing it trades out of panic, greed, or revenge.
trading-psikolojisi-duygusal-kararlar.s1: "Revenge trading" after a loss — opening an unplanned, large position to recover a loss immediately — is perhaps the most destructive behavioral pattern. This is usually followed by FOMO (fear of missing out): opening a position without analysis just to "get on the train" while the price rises rapidly.

Another common mistake is closing a winning position too early (due to fear) but keeping a losing position open for too long in the hope that it will "turn around" — psychologically, accepting losses is harder than giving up gains, and this asymmetry usually leads to losing trades remaining larger than winning trades.
trading-psikolojisi-duygusal-kararlar.s2: When real money is at risk, the brain starts working with survival responses rather than rational analysis. This is not a weakness, but a part of human biology. The solution is not "stronger willpower", but building a system that does not require making decisions in emotional moments.
trading-psikolojisi-duygusal-kararlar.s3: The following habits are methods commonly used by experienced investors to prevent emotional decisions:
Define your entry, stop-loss, and target level in writing before every trade — changing a decision while a position is open is much harder than making it beforehand.
Set a maximum loss limit for a day/week and turn off the screen when you reach this limit.
Wait a specific period of time (e.g., one day) before opening a new trade right after a loss — this prevents most revenge trades.
Record your trades in a journal (trading journal): seeing which decisions were made according to the plan and which were made emotionally will be your greatest teacher over time.
There is a significant psychological difference between testing a strategy on a demo account and trading with small positions on a live account — we cover this transition in a separate article.
trading-psikolojisi-duygusal-kararlar.s4: Trading psychology is not a topic to be learned once and forgotten, but a discipline that requires continuous effort. Even the best technical analysis or risk management rules will not protect an investor who abandons them in an emotional moment.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.title: The Difference Between ECN and Market Maker Brokers
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s0.p0: Terms like "ECN", "STP", and "Market Maker" encountered when choosing a broker are often passed over without sufficient explanation. However, these terms directly affect how your orders are actually processed and your cost structure.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s1.head: How does a Market Maker (Dealing Desk) work?
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s1.p0: Market Maker brokers match client orders within their internal systems or act as the counterparty instead of routing them directly to the market. This model can offer fixed spreads and usually commission-free trading — providing an accessible structure for small accounts and beginners.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s1.p1: The criticized aspect of this model is that, theoretically, the broker is in a position to profit from client losses. With regulated, reputable brokers, this does not pose a problem — but it is important to know that pricing is based on the broker's internal pricing rather than raw market prices.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s2.head: How does ECN/STP work?
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s2.p0: ECN (Electronic Communication Network) and STP (Straight Through Processing) brokers route orders directly to a liquidity pool (banks, other investors). Prices are raw market prices, and the broker usually charges a fixed commission per lot instead of (or in addition to) a spread.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s2.p1: The advantage of this model is transparency — spreads can narrow or widen (floating spread), especially during high market activity, but the price reflects real market supply and demand. The disadvantage is that calculating total cost (spread + commission) requires slightly more attention compared to a Market Maker's "single fixed spread" pricing.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s3.head: Which model is suitable for whom?
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s3.p0: For investors starting with small accounts, seeking simplicity, and trading infrequently, the Market Maker's fixed spread + commission-free structure is generally more predictable. For active investors applying scalping or high-frequency strategies where raw spreads are more valuable than commissions, ECN/STP accounts are usually more cost-effective.
ecn-vs-market-maker-broker-farki.s3.p1: Many brokers now offer both models under different account types (for example, "Standard" and "Zero/Raw") — which requires asking the right question not as "which broker is better", but as "which account type suits my trading style". ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.title: How to Read an Economic Calendar: Market-Moving Data
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s0.p0: The economic calendar is one of the most practical tools showing the reason behind most price movements in the forex market. However, looking at dozens of data releases on the calendar without knowing which ones are truly important often turns into a confusing pile of noise.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s1.heading: Understanding impact levels
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s1.p0: Most economic calendars classify data into low/medium/high impact (usually with yellow/orange/red color codes). High-impact data includes central bank interest rate decisions, inflation reports (CPI), and US non-farm payrolls (NFP) data — these usually cause sudden and sharp price movements the moment they are released.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.heading: Most followed data
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.p0: The following data points are the most decisive for most currency pairs:
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.l0: Interest rate decisions — whether central banks raise policy interest rates directly affects the currency's appeal.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.l1: Inflation data (CPI/PCE) — is one of the strongest signals regarding the central bank's future interest rate decisions.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.l2: Employment reports — particularly NFP in the US, are considered a strong indicator of the overall health of the economy.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.l3: GDP growth figures — show the general direction of the economy and are usually the reason behind slower but sustainable trends.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s2.l4: Speeches by central bank governors — signals given regarding future policy move the market just as much as the numbers themselves.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s3.heading: The difference between expectation and actual is important
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s3.p0: The market reacts more to how much the data deviates from expectations than to the data itself. If inflation comes in higher than expected (when the market expected lower), this can generally lead to a strengthening of that currency — because the probability increases that the central bank will keep interest rates higher for longer. The difference between expected and actual is more decisive than the absolute value of the number.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s4.heading: Things to consider around high-impact data
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s4.l0: Spreads can widen immediately before and after data releases — opening positions during this period can be extra costly.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s4.l1: The sharp movement in the first few minutes usually reflects the market's initial reaction rather than the true direction; waiting for it to settle can be healthier.
ekonomik-takvim-nasil-okunur.s4.l2: Reducing position size or reviewing stop-loss orders prior to high-impact data is a reasonable precaution against unexpected volatility.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.title: Transitioning from Demo to Real Account: When and How?
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s0.p0: A demo account is the best way to test a platform and strategy risk-free — but many investors who are profitable for months on a demo account experience an unexpected performance drop when they switch to a real account. The reason for this is usually not the strategy, but the psychological difference brought by real money risk.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s1.hea: The main difference between a demo and a real account: emotion, not money
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s1.p0: In a demo account, a loss is just a number. In a real account, the same loss creates anxiety, regret, and the desire to react impulsively — which is exactly the dynamic we addressed in our trading psychology article. This difference can have a much larger impact on performance than thought; even if the strategy remains the same, the behavior of the person executing it changes.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s2.hea: Signs showing you are ready for the transition
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s2.l0: You have tested your strategy in a demo account for a long enough period (several weeks-months, not just a few days) and under different market conditions.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s2.l1: You can execute your risk management rules (position sizing, stop-loss placement) automatically, without hesitation.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s2.l2: You see a consistent pattern in your trading journal — a repeatable process rather than random gains/losses.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s3.hea: A practical way to smooth the transition
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s3.p0: Instead of trading at normal size right away, starting a real account with a very small position size (for example, one-tenth of what you planned) is a reasonable intermediate step. This limits potential losses while experiencing the psychological impact of real money risk. Over time, as results remain consistent with your demo performance, position size can be gradually increased.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s3.p1: When choosing a broker, remember that account types offering a low minimum deposit amount are particularly suitable for this gradual transition — you can examine these criteria in more detail on our broker comparison page.
demo-hesaptan-gercek-hesaba-gecis.s4.p0: Results achieved in a demo account are not a guarantee that they will be replicated one-to-one in a real account — in either direction. The goal is not a perfect prediction, but observing your own behavior when facing real money risk and making adjustments as needed.
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.title: What is Swap (Overnight Interest)? How to Reduce Your Costs?
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s0.p0: Spread and commission are the first things that come to mind when talking about forex costs — but for traders who hold their positions open for more than a day, swap (overnight interest) is also a frequently overlooked cost item that needs to be taken into account.
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s1.heading: What is swap, why does it exist?
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s1.p0: In Forex, every trade is essentially buying one currency and selling another. Due to the difference between the interest rates of the two currencies, if you hold your position open past midnight (the cutoff time set by the broker), this interest rate differential is reflected in your account — either as positive (earning) or negative (cost).
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s1.p1: For example, if you buy a currency with a low interest rate and sell a currency with a high interest rate, you generally pay negative swap; in the opposite case, you can earn positive swap. This varies depending on the pair and position direction (long/short).
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s2.heading: Who is swap important for, and who is it not?
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s2.p0: For traders who trade intraday and close positions before the cutoff time, swap is virtually irrelevant. But for traders who hold positions for days, weeks, or even months (swing or position trading), swap can become a significant part of the total cost/gain — especially in currency pairs with a high interest rate differential.
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s3.heading: How can you check swap?
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s3.l0: Check your broker's swap table before opening a position — swap rates vary depending on the direction of the pair and differ from broker to broker.
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s3.l1: If you are planning a long-term position, factor in the effect of swap on the total cost in advance; a daily rate that seems small can accumulate over weeks.
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s3.l2: Brokers offering Islamic/swap-free account options may charge a fixed administration fee instead of swap — it is useful for investors who wish to avoid interest-bearing transactions for religious reasons to check this option.
swap-gecelik-faiz-nedir.s3.l3: On Wednesdays, swap usually increases to 3 times (as compensation for the weekend break) — do not forget this day when calculating your position carrying cost.
How to Build Your Own AI-Powered Market Tracking System

A professional Bloomberg terminal can cost tens of thousands of dollars a year. But what most retail investors actually need is not that complex: a reliable watchlist, a filter to make sense of incoming news, and a discipline to stick to their own rules. All three of these — when set up correctly — can be established with free tools and an artificial intelligence assistant.

What is described here is not investment advice; it is a method for setting up a system that will make your own decision-making process more organized. Artificial intelligence does not tell you what to buy or sell — you make the decision, it merely organizes the data at hand and reminds you of your own rules.
1. Set up your tracking dashboard
The first layer is a simple setup where you can see the general pulse of the market. There is no need for complex software for this:
A free charting platform for charts and indices — you can follow main indices and your own watchlist here.
A screener/heatmap tool for sector and stock movements — allows you to quickly see the winners and losers of the day.
For the news feed, your broker's news tab or RSS feeds from a few trusted sources — only headlines related to the instruments you follow.

Economic calendar — to see key dates in advance that truly move the market, such as central bank decisions, inflation, and employment data. FXPARTNER's own economic calendar page can be used for this purpose.
2. Do not trade without analyzing the news

You won't be the first to see a piece of news — algorithms react within milliseconds. Your advantage may not lie in speed, but in understanding the news better. Asking yourself four questions when faced with a new headline prevents most reactive trades:
Is this truly new information, or a repetition of previously known news?
What is the mechanism by which the news affects the price — does it affect revenue, cost, or general risk appetite?
Is the magnitude of the price movement proportionate to the importance of the news, or is it an overreaction?
Who is secondarily affected by this news? (The initial reaction usually occurs instantly in the relevant instrument; suppliers, competitors, and customers are priced in a bit more slowly.)
3. Keep your watchlist disciplined
A watchlist of 40 instruments does practically the same job as a watchlist of 0 instruments — you cannot truly focus on any of them. Dividing your list into three tiers works:
Active (3-5 instruments): Setups you are actually tracking, currently with a clear trigger level written down.
Developing (around 10): Names that are interesting but have not triggered a condition yet (like "I'll evaluate if it holds level X").
Universe (around 25): Names you understand and can trade at the right price, but are not actively monitoring right now.
4. Use the AI assistant in the right role

The most critical point here is to correctly define the role of AI: it is the analyst, you are the decision-maker. The tasks you can have an AI assistant do are concrete — organizing the data you provide, reminding you of the rules you wrote, finding patterns in your past trades. What it cannot (and should not) do is make price predictions or say "buy/sell".

A few practical use cases: asking it at the start of the day to summarize the data at hand (index futures, movements in your watchlist, the day's calendar) and give you a brief status report; asking it to pass a news item through the four-question filter above; providing a breakdown of your closed trades and asking which setups actually worked and in which ones you repeatedly made the same mistake.

FXPARTNER's own AI Market Assistant works on a similar logic — it answers market scenarios and your strategy questions, but it does not tell you which position to open with which broker. View it as a tool that accelerates your own research, not as an authority making decisions.
5. Put your risk rules in writing

This is the most overlooked part of the system, but it is the most important. An unwritten risk rule is almost always stretched under market stress. A few fundamental rules that should be put on paper (or in a notes file):
Maximum risk percentage per trade — always calculate position size based on the stop distance.
An upper limit on the number of simultaneous open positions, especially if you are newly learning.
Daily loss limit ("circuit breaker") — the rule to stop trading for the day when you reach this limit.
An invalidation condition written before opening the trade for every position: "If I lose this level, I am wrong."
The rule to test a sufficient number of trades on a demo account before starting with real money for a new strategy.
Final note

Setting up such a system does not make you a profitable investor — no system can guarantee that. What it does is make your decisions less impulsive and more traceable: allowing you to look back and see which rule generated which signal, what you did based on that signal, and what the outcome was. Test every new rule you establish on a demo account first, not with real money; no system guarantees profit, and what is described here is not investment advice.

turkiyede-forex-broker-secimi-spk-guveni: Choosing a Forex Broker in Turkey: SPK, Foreign License and Reliability Guide

For an investor wishing to trade forex/CFD from Turkey, the first and most fundamental distinction is this: is trading done through a brokerage firm based in Turkey and licensed by the Capital Markets Board (SPK), or through a broker established abroad operating under a foreign regulator? These two options are completely different from each other in terms of both legal framework and investor protection — and most confusion stems from not clearly understanding this distinction.

This guide is for general informational purposes and is not investment or legal advice. Regulations and current announcements from the SPK may change over time; we recommend that you always verify the information on this page with official sources from the SPK (spk.gov.tr) and the Turkish Capital Markets Association (TSPB, tspb.org.tr).
What does the SPK do, and whom does it regulate?

The Capital Markets Board (SPK) is the official authority regulating capital markets and investment institutions in Turkey. In order to offer leveraged trading (forex/CFD) services based in Turkey, an institution must obtain a license from the SPK. An SPK-licensed brokerage firm is subject to obligations such as segregation of customer funds, minimum capital requirements, and regular auditing — which means there is a tangible legal authority you can apply to in the event of a dispute.

The Turkish Capital Markets Association (TSPB) is the self-regulatory organization of which SPK-licensed brokerage firms are members, and it publishes an up-to-date list of member institutions on its website. The most reliable way to check whether an institution is truly SPK-licensed is to look at these two official sources, not claims.
Foreign brokers: why a different category?

The vast majority of forex brokers operating in the market are not SPK-licensed — they are companies established outside Turkey under foreign regulators such as FCA (UK), ASIC (Australia), and CySEC (Cyprus). These brokers may be completely legitimate and subject to supervision under their own regulators, but for an investor in Turkey, the situation is different: these institutions are not under the direct audit and enforcement authority of the SPK, and when a dispute arises, there is no SPK process in Turkey you can apply to.

From time to time, the SPK has issued public announcements regarding unauthorized foreign platforms marketing to Turkey-based investors and has taken decisions restricting access to certain platforms. This does not mean that every foreign broker in question is untrustworthy — many are institutions operating for decades in their home countries under tier-1 regulators — but it does mean there is an additional layer of legal uncertainty for an investor in Turkey.

Therefore, before choosing a foreign broker, it is necessary to separately research that broker's status with its own regulator (its license tier in its home country, not the SPK's in Turkey) and its current status regarding access/trading from Turkey.
Leverage, money transfer, and tax: practical differences

Leverage limits: Maximum leverage ratios applied at SPK-licensed domestic brokerage firms are determined by the regulator and are generally lower than the ratios offered by foreign offshore brokers — verify the current ratio with the SPK-licensed institution itself.

Money transfer: Deposit/withdrawal transactions made to a foreign broker are subject to the rules and foreign exchange regulations of your bank or card provider; some transactions may require additional documentation or explanation.

Tax: The status of the profits earned under Turkish tax legislation is the investor's own responsibility, regardless of where the broker is established — for up-to-date and personalized information on this matter, it is necessary to consult a tax advisor.

Complaint/dispute path: In a dispute with a domestic SPK-licensed institution, you have the opportunity to apply to the SPK and TSPB; in a dispute with an offshore broker, the complaint mechanism of that broker's own regulator applies.
Framework for evaluating a broker's reliability
Regardless of whether it is domestic or offshore, the four axes to look at when evaluating a broker are the same — this is the framework that FXPARTNER uses in its own broker comparison system:

Regulation — how many licenses does it have, in which countries, and in which tier? If you are trading domestically, check its SPK/TSPB registration; if you are trading offshore, check that country's regulatory tier.
Cost — how much do the spread, commission, overnight interest (swap), and hidden fees add up to in total?
Platform — does it support popular platforms like MT4/MT5, and can it be tested with a demo account?
Withdrawal reliability — are there recurring withdrawal complaints in independent user reviews, and are withdrawal times transparent?
Practical checklist
If you are going to work with a domestic institution, verify the institution's name from the current member list of the SPK or TSPB.

If you are going to work with an offshore broker, check that broker's regulatory license in its home country (such as FCA, ASIC, CySEC) and its tier; confirm the "licensed" claim not from the broker's own website, but from the official website of the relevant regulator.
In either case, search the broker's name on independent review sources along with the terms "complaint" and "withdrawal" to see if there is a recurring pattern.

FXPARTNER's broker comparison page scores each broker it lists individually based on regulation, cost, platform, and withdrawal performance — it can be used to see which broker is strong on which axis.
Final note

There is no single answer to the question "which is the most reliable forex broker in Turkey", because being "reliable" varies depending on the domestic/offshore distinction, your risk tolerance, and which regulatory protection you prioritize. Rather than giving you a name, this page shows you which order to ask the right questions in. Before making an investment decision, confirm the current regulatory status on the official website of the SPK, TSPB, or the relevant foreign regulator; this content does not constitute investment or legal advice.

litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s0.p0: The majority of investors who make consistent profits on a demo account for three months lose money in their first month switching to a real account. The reason is not strategy, but psychology: carrying a losing position on a demo account is free, but on a real account it is not. No demo account can teach this difference, because real money is required to teach it.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s0.p1: A cent account exists precisely to fill this gap. It is a real account — operating with real prices, real order execution, and real money — but because the account unit is cents instead of dollars, the risk scale is one hundred times smaller. You deposit 10 dollars, your balance appears as 1,000 in the terminal, and on a 0.01 lot position, your loss per pip is 10 cents instead of 10 cents.

litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s1.headin: What is a cent account technically?
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s1.p0: In a standard forex account, 1 lot is a 100,000-unit contract. In a cent account, 1 lot is 1,000 units — a contract scaled to one-tenth of a standard account's micro lot. Your balance is displayed using the same logic: the 10 dollars you deposit appears as 1,000 cents in the terminal.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s1.p1: The only change here is the scale. The spread comes from the same market, slippage occurs in the same way, overnight swap works the same way, and margin call is triggered by the same rules. Every mechanic you want to learn functions in its real form here — only the cost of making a mistake is small.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s1.p2: In LiteFinance's cent account, the minimum deposit is 10 dollars, spreads start from 3 pips, no commission is charged, and the stop out level is %50. litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s2.headin: Why a demo account is not enough
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s2.p0: The things a demo account teaches are real: using the platform, getting to know order types, reading charts, mechanically executing a strategy. The only thing it cannot teach is how you make decisions when your own money is at risk — and most of the money lost in the market comes not from strategy, but from precisely these decision moments.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s2.l0: Carrying a floating loss of 200 dollars in a demo account is emotionally free; the same loss in real money keeps you awake at night and leads you to close the position early.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s2.l1: In a demo account, it is easy to let a position reach its profit target; in real money, the urge to realize profit early is much stronger.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s2.l2: In a demo account, pulling back the stop loss level has no consequence; in a real account, this is the most common behavior that wipes out an account in a single trade.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s2.l3: In a demo account, most executed orders occur at the ideal price; in a real account, during news events, you encounter slippage and widening spreads.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.headin: First week plan: what to do in a cent account
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.p0: The goal of a cent account is not to make money, but to collect data under real conditions. If you start with a profit target, you lose all the benefits of the account — a meaningful profit in a 10 dollar account is only possible with irrational leverage, and that ruins everything you want to learn.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.l0: Days 1-2: Open the account, complete verification (KYC), deposit 10-20 dollars, and execute 3-5 trades with the smallest lot on a single pair (preferably EUR/USD). Goal: to see order execution and platform flow with real money.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.l1: Days 3-5: Write down stop loss and take profit levels in advance for every trade, and do not change any of them once the trade is opened. Goal: to measure the urge to break the plan.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.l2: Days 6-7: Keep a trading journal — reason for entry, reason for exit, how you felt during the trade. These three columns are the actual output of the cent account.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.l3: Throughout the week: Determine position size by calculation, not estimation. FXPARTNER's position size calculator tells you how many lots you need to open based on account balance and stop loss distance.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s3.l4: Do not: Pull leverage to 1:1000 and try to double the account. If you do this in a cent account, the only thing you will learn is how quickly the account gets wiped out.
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s4.headin: When to exit a cent account?
litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s4.p0: A cent account is a stepping stone, not a destination. The right signal for exiting is not profit, but consistency: if you can see from your own journal over a series of at least 30-40 trades that you stuck to your plan and the results were not accidental, you can move on to the next step.

litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s5.l2: The psychology of a cent account is not full-scale. Losing 10 dollars does not feel the same as losing 1.000 dollars — a cent account teaches the beginning of emotional pressure, not all of it.

litefinance-cent-hesap-rehberi.s6.l4: Start with an amount you can afford to lose. This applies to every account type, including cent accounts.

litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.title: Instant Withdrawal at LiteFinance: Three Conditions and Real Times
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s0.p0: In Forex, the most honest signal a broker gives you is withdrawals. Depositing money is fast at every broker — they want to take the money. The real test is what happens when you ask for that money back.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s0.p1: LiteFinance has a good profile in this test: on a verified account with automated withdrawal flow enabled, requests are processed instantly — up to 5.000 dollars a day on supported methods, multiple times during the day, without waiting for manual approval. litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s0.p2: This article explains those three conditions, how long each method actually takes, and the most common mistakes made on the first withdrawal. As conditions may change, verify the figures on the broker's official website before opening an account.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s1.heading: Three conditions for instant withdrawal
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s1.p0: Instant withdrawal is not a privilege, it is a configuration. It works when you fulfill all three, and fails when you leave one out — and most users learn which one is missing on the day they try to withdraw money.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s1.l0: 1. Account verification (KYC) must be completed. ID and proof of address are uploaded from the cabinet. No withdrawal is processed automatically on an unverified account. Take care of this on the day you deposit, not the day you want to withdraw.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s1.l1: 2. Automatic withdrawal must be enabled in the cabinet. This is a setting and may not come enabled by default. Check it in your personal cabinet.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s1.l2: 3. The withdrawal method must support this flow. Cards and e-wallets support it. Wire transfer naturally does not support it — the money goes through a correspondent banking chain, and no broker can speed up this chain.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.heading: Real times per method
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.p0: The times below cover the time it takes for the money to reach you, not the time it takes for the broker to process the request — the two are different, and most complaints stem from this difference. The broker can process the request in 30 seconds, but your e-wallet provider might hold it for 2 hours on their side.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.l0: E-wallet (in automatic flow): instant — mostly within minutes. The daily automated limit of 5.000 dollars becomes most meaningful in this channel.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.l1: Bank/credit card: processed instantly on the broker side, but depending on the refund process of the card network, it may take 1-5 business days to reflect on your account. This delay stems from the card scheme, not the broker.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.l2: Crypto transfer: depends on network confirmation time, usually minutes. Network fee is your responsibility.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.l3: Bank wire transfer: 1-3 business days. It is outside the automated flow.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s2.l4: Requests over 5,000 dollars and everything outside the automated flow: mostly within 24 hours, processed manually.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s3.heading: Same method rule — the item that causes the most surprises
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s3.p0: At LiteFinance, money can only be withdrawn using the same method and currency you deposited with. If you deposited with Skrill, you can only withdraw to the same Skrill wallet; if you deposited with a card, the refund goes to that card first.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s3.p1: This is not an arbitrary restriction, but a standard requirement of anti-money laundering regulations and is common in the industry. But in practice, it means: when choosing your deposit method, you are actually choosing your withdrawal method as well. Depositing with a card you do not use or a wallet you have uncertain access to is a decision that is troublesome to fix later.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s3.p2: If you deposited using multiple methods, withdrawals are usually distributed proportionally to the deposited amounts. This explains why setting up your account around a single method creates less friction.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s4.heading: Fees: where does %0-2 come from?

litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s4.p1: Practical result: withdrawing 1,000 dollars once a month can be cheaper than withdrawing 250 dollars four times. If you make frequent and small withdrawals, calculate the fee per method once; the annual total turns out higher than most people expect.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s5.heading: Five most common mistakes in the first withdrawal
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s5.l0: Trying to do KYC on the day you want to withdraw money. Document approval takes time; most of the "instant withdrawal is not working" complaints are actually this.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s5.l1: Submitting a withdrawal request from an account with an active bonus. Bonus is extra margin; a withdrawal request usually leads to the cancellation of the bonus and the profit derived from it. Read the bonus terms before withdrawing.

litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s5.l4: Trying the first withdrawal with a large amount. Making the first withdrawal with a small amount at a new broker and seeing the process from start to finish is a common-sense rule applicable to every broker.
litefinance-anlik-para-cekme.s6.heading: Withdrawal speed is a measure of trust — but not enough on its own

litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.title: What Are You Really Paying Per Lot? ECN Cost Calculation
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s0.p0: The most common misleading statement in forex ads is "spread from 0.0 pips". It is not wrong — but incomplete. Every account offering a 0.0 pip spread takes the cost as commission, and a comparison that ignores commission always makes the wrong account look cheap.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s0.p1: The right question is: how many dollars in total do I pay when I open and close the same trade? In this article, we perform that calculation step by step across three account types. The figures used are the starting values declared by the brokers and are subject to change; confirm from the broker's official website before trading for your own account.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s1.p0: In EUR/USD, 1 standard lot is 100,000 units, and 1 pip at this size equals approximately 10 dollars. So to convert the spread into dollars, simply multiply the spread in pips by 10.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s1.p1: There is a single detail to pay attention to on the commission side, and it can double the cost: whether the commission is one-way (per side) or round-trip (round turn). The expression "$3.50 per lot, per side" means that opening and closing a position costs $7. If you do not look for these two words when reading a broker's commission figure, every comparison you make will be flawed.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s1.p2: There is a third item: swap if you carry a position overnight. If you are day trading, swap does not concern you; if you carry a position for a few days, on some pairs swap can be larger than the total of spread and commission.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s2.headin: Three accounts, one trade: 1 lot EUR/USD open-close
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s2.p0: The calculation below is made assuming the spread is at its stated starting value. In reality, 0.0 pip is a baseline value, not an average — under normal session conditions on ECN-type accounts, the EUR/USD spread mostly moves in the range of 0.1-0.5 pip. To keep the comparison honest, we assumed an average of 0.3 pip on ECN accounts.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s2.l0: LiteFinance Classic — spread 1.8 pip, no commission. Cost: 1.8 × $10 = $18.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s2.l1: LiteFinance ECN — spread ~0.3 pip + commission starting from $0.25 per lot. Cost: $3 + $0.25-0.50 = approximately $3.25-3.50.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s2.l2: XM Zero — spread ~0.3 pip + $3.50 commission per lot per side. Cost: $3 + $7 = approximately $10.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s2.l3: XM Standard — spread 1.0 pip, no commission. Cost: 1.0 × $10 = $10.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s3.p0: First: a commission-free account does not mean a cheap account. LiteFinance Classic is the only "no commission" option on this list and at the same time the most expensive — because the cost is removed from commission and embedded into the spread. The appeal of commission-free accounts lies not in cost, but in the simplicity of the account.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s3.p1: Second: there can be up to a threefold cost difference between two different brokers' "0.0 pip ECN" accounts. The difference here comes not from the spread, but from the commission structure — the gap between LiteFinance's commission starting from $0.25 per lot and XM Zero's $3.50 per side determines whether you execute the same trade for $3.50 or $10.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s3.p2: Third: the difference grows with volume. For someone trading 50 lots a month, the per-lot difference of approximately $14.50 between Classic and ECN equates to $725 a month. This is an item larger than the annual return expectations of most retail accounts, and it is entirely related to the choice of account type.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s4.headin: How does cashback change the calculation?
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s4.p0: Transaction cost is not a one-way item: a portion of it can come back via the share the broker pays to its partner. On LiteFinance accounts linked via FXPARTNER, the cashback rate goes up to 50% — calculated on commission for ECN accounts, and on spread for Classic and Cent accounts.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s4.p1: In practice, this means that a portion of the ECN cost above is returned. Since the size of the rebate depends on the account type and monthly volume, it would not be accurate to give a single figure; but the direction is clear: the rebate makes the account that is already the cheapest even cheaper, and its effect increases as volume grows.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s4.p2: Important detail: you do not need to close your existing account for cashback. It is sufficient to submit your account number through FXPARTNER's cashback page; the rebate is deposited directly into your trading account by the broker based on your trading volume.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s5.headin: Which account is suitable for whom?
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s5.l0: If you trade under 5 lots per month: the cost difference is small in absolute terms (approximately $70). If account simplicity is more valuable to you, a commission-free account is a reasonable choice.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s5.l1: Between 5-50 lots per month: an ECN-type account is clearly cheaper, and the difference becomes visible in your monthly budget.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s5.l2: Scalping or high-frequency trading: an option other than ECN makes practically no sense. In this style, total cost directly determines the profitability threshold of the strategy.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s5.l3: If you carry positions (a few days-weeks): your priority is not spread or commission, but swap rates. Make your cost comparison based on swap.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s5.l4: If you use an expert advisor (EA): run your backtests with your account's actual spread and commission. Many EAs that appear profitable with default test settings turn unprofitable when actual costs are entered.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s6.l0: Verify whether the commission is per side or round-trip — this single question can double the cost.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s6.l1: Measure the average spread during the hours you trade, not the stated minimum. Recording the spread on a demo account for a week is sufficient.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s6.l2: Calculate with the instrument you trade. Pip value and typical spread are completely different for gold, indices, and exotic pairs.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s6.l3: Multiply by your monthly volume. A difference of a few dollars per lot can reach an amount comparable to your account size in the annual total.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s6.l4: Deduct cashback from the net cost if available — but treat the rebate not as a profit, but as a cost reduction.
litefinance-ecn-maliyet-hesabi.s7.p0: Trading cost is one of the very few variables a trader can control. You cannot predict the direction of the market, but you can know exactly what you pay per lot and reduce it — and in the long run, this makes a bigger difference than many strategy improvements.

forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.title: Why Can't You Withdraw Your Bonus? The Mathematics of the Volume Requirement
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s0.p0: "100% deposit bonus" is the most effective marketing phrase in this industry, and also the most misunderstood. Most new traders think the bonus is money added to the balance. It is not. A bonus is a conditional margin credit that cannot be withdrawn until specific conditions are met.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s0.p1: This article is brand-independent — the mechanics described work the same way in almost every broker that offers bonuses. To make the examples concrete, we use the bonus types published by LiteFinance, but numbers change periodically; read the current terms on the broker's official website before joining.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s1.p0: A bonus is an amount included in your account's margin calculation but not included in your withdrawable balance. When you deposit 500 dollars and receive a 100% bonus, you see 1,000 dollars in the terminal; 500 of this 1,000 dollars is yours, and 500 is the broker's conditional contribution.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s1.p1: The only concrete thing this provides you is more margin room: you get caught in a margin call later for the same position size. What it does not provide is profit potential — the bonus does not increase the earnings of your positions, it only allows you to open larger positions. The difference between these two explains why a bonus is a risk multiplier.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s1.p2: Types commonly seen at LiteFinance: 30% bonus on deposits over 50 dollars, and 100% bonus on deposits over 100 dollars with a promo code. Bonuses are usually valid for 6 months and carry a maximum cap amount.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.headin: How is the volume requirement calculated?
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.p0: For the bonus (and in most cases, the profit originating from the bonus) to become withdrawable, you need to complete a certain trading volume. This volume is expressed in lots and is usually calculated with a multiplier linked to the bonus amount.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.p1: The following example is not a real campaign condition, but a calculation set up to demonstrate the mechanism. Read the multiplier of your own campaign from the terms page and do the same calculation.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.l0: Assumption: You deposited 500 dollars, and received 500 dollars in bonus with a 100% bonus. Suppose the campaign sets a requirement of 1 lot traded for every 1 dollar of bonus.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.l1: Required volume: 500 lots. In EUR/USD, 500 standard lots means a nominal trading volume of 50 million dollars.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.l2: Cost of this volume: On an account with a 1.8 pip spread, approximately 18 dollars per lot × 500 lots = 9,000 dollars in trading costs.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.l3: Result: To make a 500 dollar bonus withdrawable, you need to pay 9,000 dollars in costs. Under this condition, the bonus is mathematically not something worth taking.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s2.l4: Do the same calculation on a campaign with a low multiplier — for example 0.1 lots for every 1 dollar of bonus — and the figure drops to 50 lots and the cost to 900 dollars. The decision lies entirely in the multiplier.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s3.headin: The unseen cost of a bonus: behavioral change
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s3.p0: The real price of the volume requirement is not the spread you pay, but the behavior it pushes you into. A trader trying to complete the requirement opens trades even when their strategy does not give a signal — because their goal is no longer to make good trades, but to accumulate lots.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s3.p1: This is one of the most systematic ways to blow an account in forex, and the cause is not the bonus, but the incentive created by the bonus. The same trader would make 10 trades a month if they did not get a bonus; with the bonus, they make 60 trades, and the expected value of these 50 extra trades is negative.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s3.p2: The second unseen cost: at most brokers, the bonus is canceled upon a withdrawal request. So if you want to withdraw money while you have an active bonus on your account, you lose the bonus and in most cases the profit originating from the bonus. This is a real loss for someone in need of urgent cash.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s4.headin: When does a bonus make sense?
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s4.p0: A bonus is not always bad — when its conditions are read correctly, it works in certain situations.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s4.l0: If there is a requirement close to the volume you would already trade. For someone trading 40 lots a month, a 50-lot requirement is an achievable target without changing their behavior.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s4.l1: If you plan to use the bonus only as a margin buffer rather than withdrawing it — and if you do not allow this buffer to let you increase your position size.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s4.l2: If the duration of the bonus (usually 6 months) aligns with your normal trading pace.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s4.l3: And in any case: if the bonus is not the reason you choose the broker. Broker selection is made based on regulation, cost, platform, and withdrawals; a bonus does not compensate for any of these four.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s5.headin: Five lines to read in bonus terms
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s5.l0: Volume multiplier: how many lots for every $1 of bonus? This single figure determines whether the bonus is achievable.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s5.l1: Which instruments count toward volume? In some campaigns, only certain pairs or positions held longer than a specific duration count.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s5.l2: How much is the bonus cap? Even if the percentage looks large, the absolute cap is often low.

forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s5.l4: Does a withdrawal request cancel the bonus? Almost always yes — but do not assume without seeing the exact phrasing of the condition.
forex-bonus-tuzagi-hacim-sarti.s6.p0: A bonus is not free money, but a conditional margin credit, and its true cost is written in the volume requirement. trump-clarity-act-cagrisi-kripto-yukseli: On August 19, 2026, US President Donald Trump met with leading figures of the crypto industry at the Eisenhower Building on the White House campus and called on the Senate to pass the crypto market structure legislation known as the CLARITY Act. Top executives from companies such as Coinbase, Ripple, Gemini, Robinhood, Polymarket, and Kalshi, as well as leadership from the SEC and CFTC, attended the meeting.

The market reaction was sharp. Bitcoin briefly rose above 70,000 dollars for the first time since June 2, Ethereum rose by double digits in a single session, and the total crypto market capitalization rose above 2.3 trillion dollars.

The purpose of this article is not to repeat the headline, but to clarify two things: the legislation has not been passed yet, and Trump's statement is not the sole reason for the rally. We address both in turn.
What happened in the market: August 19-20 numbers

The numbers here belong to the August 19-20 sessions and diverge because different sources provide different snapshots — while some publications report the peak around 71,800 dollars, measurements closer to the close show a range of 68,000-69,000 dollars. This is not a contradiction, but different hours of the same day. When trading, your sole reference should be the live price on your own platform.
Bitcoin: traded in the 68,000-69,700 dollar range, spilling over 70,000 dollars at the intraday peak; the 24-hour change is roughly between +5% and +7% depending on the source and time.
Ethereum: reclaimed the 2,000 dollar level and rose up to around 2,250 dollars; daily gain in the 17-18% range.
Solana: approximately 85 dollars, daily +10.8%.
XRP: approximately 1.10 dollars, daily +10.3%.
Total crypto market capitalization rose above 2.32 trillion dollars; Bitcoin dominance is around 61%.
What exactly does the CLARITY Act do?

The exact reason the industry has wanted this law for years is the first item: a clear rule, even if restrictive, is preferred to uncertainty, because uncertainty makes investment and product planning impossible.
The framework that the bill aims to introduce can be summarized under three main headings:
Clarifying at the federal level which institution will oversee which digital asset — that is, drawing the jurisdictional boundary between the SEC and the CFTC.
Establishing rules regarding registration, operation, and the protection of customer assets for crypto exchanges and brokerages.
Setting ethical limits regarding public officials issuing digital assets and earning income from them.
The bill has not been passed — timeline and actual status

This distinction needs to be underlined, as news often circulates on social media giving the impression that the bill was passed. Trump's statement on August 19 was not an approval, but a call. The bill is still pending in the Senate.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune filed a cloture motion for the bill on August 8; this step paved the way for a procedural vote to be held on September 15. However, what will be voted on there is not the passage of the bill, but whether to proceed to debate.

The numerical breakdown is as follows: 60 votes are required in the Senate for the bill to move forward, and Republicans need approximately six Democratic votes. The bill passed the Senate Banking Committee in May with support from only two Democrats, and that gap has not closed since then.

Ethics provisions: A regulation stipulating the prohibition of public officials and their spouses from issuing digital assets. The compromise text prepared by Senators Ruben Gallego and Thom Tillis also mandates that Trump divest from his stakes in crypto companies; Trump has not yet approved this text. According to the disclosure released in June, the president's income from crypto ventures in 2025 was close to 1.2 billion dollars.
Lack of agreement on combating illicit finance and the scope of law enforcement powers.
The debate over whether stablecoins can distribute yield or rewards to users — a topic heavily lobbied by the banking sector.
Three catalysts behind the rise

The third point is particularly important. A short squeeze is not a story of demand, but a story of forced buying: rising prices force investors who bet downward to buy in order to close their positions, these purchases push the price even higher, and the cycle feeds itself. Such moves come quickly; when the catalyst is exhausted and forced buying ends, they can be given back just as quickly.
Policy signal: Trump's call for the CLARITY Act and, a day earlier, on 18 August, the SEC's proposal of a draft rule directly targeting token issuances for the first time.

Macro: The US Treasury increased its long-term bond buybacks from $2 billion to $4 billion per transaction. The 30-year bond yield declined from 5.337% to 5.18%, and this easing in interest rates directly increased demand for risk assets.
Mechanics: short position liquidation. Approximately $1.7-1.9 billion worth of positions were liquidated within 24 hours, the overwhelming majority of which were short positions.

In other words, the rally on 19 August was not merely the pricing of a regulatory expectation, but a movement compounded by leverage liquidation. This distinction determines how confident you can be regarding the permanence of the move.
Three scenarios for 15 September

Here, a classic pattern needs to be noted: buy the rumor, sell the news. In regulatory processes, prices often rise during the expectation phase and pull back when the news occurs, even if the outcome is positive. This is not a rule, but a frequently repeated behavioral pattern.

Procedural vote passes: The bill enters the Senate agenda. This does not mean the law is passed, but it reduces uncertainty. The expected reaction is positive; however, since the news is partially priced in, it is common to see profit-taking following the initial reaction.

Procedural vote fails: The 60-vote threshold is not reached, and the process returns to uncertainty. Giving back a portion of the August rally is the most likely scenario; in this case, the severity of the decline is determined this time by the liquidation of leveraged long positions.

A compromise is reached by softening provisions: Progress is made by flexing ethics clauses or the stablecoin topic. This is generally the most positive scenario for the market, as both the calendar moves forward and the jurisdictional clarity desired by the industry is preserved.
If you are going to trade on this news

The most common mistake in news-driven moves is correctly predicting the direction but miscalculating the position size. There are many trades that result in a loss because interim volatility triggered the stop loss level despite the direction being correct.

Reduce your position size relative to normal sessions; when volatility increases, the same lot size no longer represents the same risk. The position size calculator on our website allows you to make this adjustment according to your account.
Lower your leverage. The reason for the liquidation exceeding $1.7 billion on 19 August was not a directional error, but the leverage level.
Assume that spreads will widen during announcement hours and plan your entries to tolerate this widening.
Mark 15 September on your calendar. Our economic calendar page allows you to see such planned events in advance; getting caught unprepared for non-surprising volatility is unnecessary.
Do not trade based on a single headline. As in the example of the three catalysts above, the cause of a move is often more than it appears.
Conclusion

What happened on 19 August is clear: Trump met with the crypto sector at the White House and called on the Senate to approve the CLARITY Act; the market priced this with a strong rally alongside bond buybacks and a massive short squeeze. What did not happen is equally clear: the law was not passed, the vote on 15 September is merely a procedural step, and the three fundamental disputes ahead of the bill remain unresolved.

Not confusing these two sentences is the most valuable position that can be taken on this news. As FXPARTNER, we will continue to follow the process and share developments ahead of the 15 September vote.
